lead: Mechanical systems move in straight lines or rotate. Newton's second law and its rotational twin turn forces and torques into differential equations. Mass stores kinetic energy, a spring stores elastic energy, and a damper removes energy. With zero initial conditions, the Laplace transform gives a transfer function. Engineers use these models for vehicle suspension, robot arms, motor shafts and door closers. Translational elements are mass m in kg, spring k in N/m and damper c in N·s/m. Rotational elements are inertia J in kg·m², torsional spring kt in N·m/rad and torsional damper b in N·m·s/rad. This chapter builds the equations and transfer functions.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for Laplace transforms and zero initial conditions, and basic Newton's laws.

blocks.text: Translational motion is along a straight line. Displacement x is in metres (m), measured from the rest position. Velocity is x′ in m/s and acceleration is x″ in m/s². A mass m in kg stores kinetic energy and gives inertia. A spring k in N/m stores elastic energy; its force on the mass is −k x when x is the extension. A viscous damper c in N·s/m removes energy; its force is −c x′, opposing velocity. Some syllabi call c the damping coefficient.
m x″ + c x′ + k x = F(t)
blocks.where: m is mass in kg; c is viscous damping coefficient in N·s/m; k is spring stiffness in N/m; x is displacement in m; F(t) is external force in N; x′ and x″ are first and second time derivatives.

items: Draw the free-body diagram: mass as a point, external force F(t) in the positive direction.
Draw spring force −k x and damper force −c x′ opposite to the chosen positive motion.
Write Newton's second law: ΣF = m x″.
Collect terms to get m x″ + c x′ + k x = F(t).
Set zero initial conditions and take the Laplace transform.

blocks.text: If gravity acts, measure x from the static equilibrium position. The weight then cancels the initial spring deflection, so mg does not appear in the equation.

Rotational motion uses angle θ in radians (rad). Angular velocity is θ′ in rad/s and angular acceleration is θ″ in rad/s². Inertia J in kg·m² is the rotational mass. A torsional spring kt in N·m/rad gives torque −kt θ. A torsional damper b in N·m·s/rad gives torque −b θ′. External torque T(t) is in N·m. Newton's second law for rotation is ΣT = J θ″.
J θ″ + b θ′ + kt θ = T(t)
blocks.where: J is moment of inertia in kg·m²; b is torsional damping in N·m·s/rad; kt is torsional stiffness in N·m/rad; θ is angle in rad; T(t) is external torque in N·m.

sections.h3: Transfer functions with zero initial conditions

blocks.text: Take the Laplace transform with zero initial conditions: x(0) = 0, x′(0) = 0, θ(0) = 0 and θ′(0) = 0. Then L{x″} = s²X(s), L{x′} = sX(s) and L{x} = X(s). The translational equation becomes (m s² + c s + k)X(s) = F(s). The rotational equation becomes (J s² + b s + kt)Θ(s) = T(s).
G(s) = X(s)/F(s) = 1/(m s² + c s + k)
blocks.where: G(s) is the transfer function in m/N; X(s) is the Laplace transform of displacement; F(s) is the Laplace transform of force; s is the Laplace variable.
Θ(s) is the Laplace transform of angle; T(s) is the Laplace transform of torque; the ratio has units rad/(N·m).

blocks.text: The denominator is the characteristic polynomial. Write it as s² + 2ζω<sub>n</sub>s + ω<sub>n</sub>². For translation, ω<sub>n</sub> = √(k/m) rad/s and ζ = c/(2√(km)). For rotation, ω<sub>n</sub> = √(kt/J) rad/s and ζ = b/(2√(kt J)). ζ has no unit. The transfer function is valid only for zero initial conditions; nonzero initial values add extra terms to the numerator.

examples.question: A mass m = 2 kg rests on a horizontal surface. It is connected to a spring k = 8 N/m and a viscous damper c = 2 N·s/m. An external force F(t) acts on the mass. Neglect friction. Find the transfer function X(s)/F(s), the natural frequency and the damping ratio.
steps: Data: m = 2 kg, c = 2 N·s/m, k = 8 N/m. Input is F(t) in N; output is x(t) in m.
Free-body diagram: take x positive to the right. External force F acts to the right. Spring force is −8x N. Damper force is −2x′ N.
Newton's second law: ΣF = m x″ gives 2x″ = F − 2x′ − 8x.
Set zero initial conditions and take Laplace transforms: (2s² + 2s + 8)X(s) = F(s).
Divide numerator and denominator by 2: X(s)/F(s) = 0.5/(s² + s + 4).
examples.answer: The transfer function is X(s)/F(s) = 1/(2s² + 2s + 8) = 0.5/(s² + s + 4) m/N, with natural frequency 2 rad/s and damping ratio 0.25.

traps: Sign slip: in ΣF = m x″ the spring and damper forces oppose motion. Writing +k x or +c x′ on the left gives wrong dynamics and often an unstable model.
Unit mix-up: c is N·s/m, not N/m; J is kg·m², not kg; kt is N·m/rad; θ is radians, not degrees.
Using the transfer function with nonzero initial conditions. G(s) is defined with zero initial displacement and zero initial velocity; extra initial-value terms change the output.
Forgetting static equilibrium when gravity acts. Measure x from the equilibrium position, otherwise mg appears twice or with the wrong sign.
Treating mass as weight. m is in kg; weight mg is a force in N and belongs on the force side only if you do not shift to equilibrium.

quiz.q: Define the viscous damping coefficient c and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: c relates damper force to velocity by F = c v. Its unit is N·s/m.

quiz.q: Why does the spring force carry a negative sign in m x″ + c x′ + k x = F(t)?
quiz.a: The spring force opposes displacement. If x is positive, the spring pulls back in the negative direction. Moving −k x to the left side gives +k x.

quiz.q: A rotational system has J = 0.5 kg·m², b = 0.2 N·m·s/rad and kt = 2 N·m/rad. Find Θ(s)/T(s) with zero initial conditions.
quiz.a: Θ/T = 1/(0.5s² + 0.2s + 2) = 2/(s² + 0.4s + 4). Natural frequency is 2 rad/s and damping ratio is 0.1.

quiz.q: A student models a system as m x″ − c x′ + k x = F with c > 0. What physical effect does the middle term describe?
quiz.a: The term −c x′ is negative damping. It adds energy instead of removing it, so oscillations grow. A passive viscous damper must give +c x′ after collecting terms.

quiz.q: Give the SI units of J and kt.
quiz.a: J is in kg·m². kt is in N·m/rad.

quiz.q: A translational system has m = 4 kg, c = 0 and k = 16 N/m. Find the natural frequency.
Why do translational and rotational systems give the same second-order transfer function shape?
quiz.a: Both have one inertia element, one spring element and one damper element. Force maps to torque, mass to inertia, x to θ, k to kt and c to b. The energy storage and loss structure is the same.

quiz.q: What happens to X(s)/F(s) if the mass starts with nonzero displacement x(0) and nonzero velocity x′(0)?
quiz.a: Laplace transform of x″ adds −s x(0) − x′(0), and x′ adds −x(0). The ratio X(s)/F(s) is no longer the pure transfer function; extra initial-condition terms appear in the numerator.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, quarter-car models use two mass-spring-damper chains to design suspension, and robot joints use J, b and kt to tune servo gains. Search 'mass-spring-damper transfer function', 'rotational inertia gear reflection' and 'modal analysis' for the next layer. Newer curricula add bond graphs, which keep power flow visible across domains.
